payload.rationale: No current data were supplied, so this rests on background knowledge with a real information gap through the September 2026 cutoff. Observed context (from memory, pre-2026): CDC counted roughly 2,200 US measles cases in 2025, the highest since 1992, driven by the West Texas outbreak, and late 2025 saw new sustained outbreaks (South Carolina Upstate, Utah/Arizona) carrying into 2026. Early 2026 reporting appeared to run well ahead of 2025's pace (several hundred cases by late January, near or above 1,000 by roughly February–March), implying a 2026 total plausibly in the 3,000–5,000 range if incidence followed typical spring peak and summer/fall decline. Exceeding 6,000 requires roughly triple the 2025 total—achievable only if multiple large under-vaccinated-community outbreaks persisted or new ones ignited in the fall, or if the US lost elimination status with broad endemic-like spread. That is possible given declining MMR coverage, but not the central case. Too-high risk: the early-2026 surge may have burned out by summer (as Texas did in 2025), leaving totals near 3,000–4,000; my recollection of early-2026 counts may be inflated. Too-low risk: I lack data from March–September 2026; if transmission persisted across many states through summer (as the accelerating trend suggested), 6,000 could already be exceeded or clearly within reach by the cutoff, and CDC totals are only revised upward as jurisdictions report. Settlement uses CDC's count as of expiration, so reporting lag slightly favors NO. Net estimate ~30%.
limitations: No supplied evidence; no access to CDC 2026 case counts through the September 2026 cutoff.
Early-2026 figures cited are from memory and may be imprecise.
Outcome depends on outbreak dynamics in late 2026 that cannot be observed here.
CDC count revisions after expiration are excluded; reporting lag could affect settlement.
